messages.subject: Grouping strategies and goodness of fit for point count data
messages.subject_clean: Grouping strategies and goodness of fit for point count data
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
   I am working on a study of songbirds in western
juniper woodlands in central Oregon.  I have collected
two seasons of point count data and am beginning to use
program DISTANCE to estimate densities of individual
bird species among different vegetative cover types.
   In the field, distances were visually estimated.
Within 20m of the point, distances were recorded to the
nearest meter.  From 20-100m from the point, distances
were recorded to the nearest 5m.  Detections greater
than 100m were recorded to the nearest ten meters.
Flagging was tied at known distances from each point to
facilitate more accurate estimation of distances.

My questions deal with three related issues:

1) I am unsure whether to analyze my data as ungrouped
or grouped.
   My distance data were essentially collected as
ungrouped in the field (ignoring the fact that all data
are grouped, depending on how fine the scale at which
the data are collected).  Buckland et al. (1993)
recommend grouping ungrouped data when heaping and
evasive movement are present.  Indeed, these problems
are present in some of my data sets.  However, are there
any other compelling reasons to group data prior to
fitting a number of models?

2)How much emphasis should be placed on the goodness of
fit tests as a means of evaluating choice of
grouping cutpoints, as well as determining whether to
analyze data as grouped or ungrouped?  (Note: this
procedure is being conducted in the exploratory phase
prior to model selection)
   My experience has shown that fitting an initial,
arbitrary model (eg. half-norm/cosine) to ungrouped data
often results in a very poor fit (p<0.0000, from
chi-square goodness of fit tests).  Subsequent grouping
of my data results in vastly improved fit.

3)Is there such a thing as an objective grouping
strategy?
   I have been able to vastly improve the fit of a given
model (evaluated by chi-square goodness of fit) by
grouping my data with a single, standardized set of
distance intervals.  The group intervals are narrow near
the point and increase at an increasing rate at further
distances from the point.  Applying this grouping
criteria to data from a number of species has
consistently resulted in excellent fits.  For most
species in my study, five to six grouping intervals
encompass all observations, and truncation is often not
necessary.
   To me, applying this standardized groups seems better
than endlessly adjusting cutpoints in order to obtain
the best chi-square p-value.  What do you think?

   In addition to replies posted on the discussion list,
I would welcome insights and/or replies to my personal
e-mail address: rein...@mailbox.orst.edu.  I would be
happy to summarize any replies for the discussion list.
   Thank you.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

messages.subject: Query: Distance error 13
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance users,

Query:

Has anyone out there ever experienced a run time error 13 (Incompatible
types) while running Distance?  If so, can you please contact me.  Also,
please contact me if you're successfully running Distance 3.5 in Uruguay or
Argentina.  Thanks!

Rationale: (for those who think they can help)

Three people have now contacted me with the following kind of problem:

> >I cannot open nor create a new file. When I click "open" or "create", a
> >warning box appears saying in Spanish: "Error '13' en tiempo de
> >ejecuci˘n. No coinciden los tipos". Then, if I click "accept", the
> >program quits unespectedly.

Two of these people were from Uruguay and one from Argentina, so I suspect
the problem must be with a local version of Windows or a local application --
however since I can't reproduce the problem on my machine here then I can't
work out how to fix it!  So, I'd like to hear from anyone who has had this
problem and fixed it, or who is successfully running Distance on a machine in
either of these two countries.  Perhaps by comparing systems, we can work out
what the problem is...

Background: (for those interested in why the problem occurs)

The fundamental problem is that modern Windows is highly modular, with many
different programs sharing the same utility files (mostly DLLs and OCXs).  If
the install routine of a program is not written exactly right it can
incorrectly overwrite some of these files, causing other programs to
malfunction.  In software jargon this situation is referred to as "DLL Hell".
This has caused problems for Distance users in the past (e.g., a badly
behaved piece of compression software), but I have managed to find fixes.
This time, however, I'm having trouble working out which piece of software is
causing the problem - and I don't have any spanish language software here to
try out.  Future versions of Distance will include a utility called a DLL
version stamper that should make diagnosing and fixing such problems much
easier.

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS

             email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
   RUWPA home page: http://www.rupwa.st-and.ac.uk
Distance home page: http://www.rupwa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

messages.subject: HELP WITH "GLIM" NEEDED
messages.body_plain:
SORRY FOR ANY CROSS-POSTINGS
Dear Distance users ,
If any of you are familiar with GLIM (4.0, I think) perhaps you can help.

We have been attempting to use GLIM to model count data and to test  the
residuals against a Poisson Distribution.  There is one response variable
and 3 explanatory variables.  We have correctly specified units, and
variables but have been unable to get the program to accept more than 25
records (or cases).  Up to 25 rows is o.k.  More than that produces an error
message that claims that the "work space is full"  Is 4 x 25, or 100 cells
really the limit or is there a way that we can read-in a substantially
larger data set?  What is the limit on the size of the data set?  Below I
have included some additional details of our design, but I do not believe
that they really relate to our problem.

There are about 124 sampling units.  The means of the response variable is
highly skewed, and resistant to transformation.  As the data, and the error
structure are so dramatically non-normal we would like to

(1) Generate a model that relates the response variable to three (3)
explanatory variables, using maximum likelihood methods;
(2) Test the residuals against a Poisson distribution;
(3) Alter the model by excluding each of the explanatory variables in turn
and testing the significance of changes in the Sum of Squares using Chi
square or, if appropriate, an F-test. (Chi square is appropriate for
Poisson).

Thanks for your help.
Eric Holt, U.Mass, Boston Master's degree candidate.
e-mail Nfi...@massed.net   This is listed as being from Nancy Fiske, but it
is from me. Thanks again.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
